title: A World Statistical Atlas of National Border Fractal Dimensions
content: This study establishes a harmonized worldwide statistical atlas of principal-landmass national border complexity, addressing the absence of any dataset estimating their fractal dimensions under one common dual-method framework. Box-counting and divider fractal dimensions were estimated for 197 countries and territories from consistently processed GADM 4.1 geometries and evaluated at continental and global levels. Most principal-landmass borders proved measurably fractal yet occupied a comparatively low complexity band, departing from the linear benchmark while remaining far from plane-filling geometry: the worldwide mean dimensions were 1.0959 and 1.0975, respectively, with no evidence of a systematic paired difference (mean difference =-0.0015 ). Cross-method correspondence was strong (Pearson r =0.9155 ; Lin CCC =0.9069 ), although Bland--Altman and rank analyses identified modest magnitude-dependent disagreement and a limited set of method-sensitive countries. The equal-weight consensus fractal dimension averaged 1.0967 worldwide, ranging from 1.0170 for Somalia to 1.3615 for Norway, and continental consensus averages were highest in North America (1.1259) and Europe (1.1150) and lowest in Africa (1.0652). With all source geometries, candidate scales, and estimates archived for replication, the country-level values form a reproducible baseline for comparative, sensitivity, and time-indexed analyses of national-border complexity.
